title: Countershading
context: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

lines.t: Today I want to look at a type of camouflage that's so common, you've probably seen it many times without noticing. It's called countershading.
Countershading means that an animal is darker on its back and lighter on its belly. Think of a shark, or a deer, or many kinds of fish.

So why would that pattern help an animal hide? Well, light usually comes from above. When sunlight hits an animal, its back is bright and its belly is in shadow. That shadow makes the animal look solid and three-dimensional, which makes it easier to see.

Countershading cancels out that effect. The dark back absorbs some of the light from above, and the pale belly brightens the shadowed part. The result is that the animal looks flatter, and it blends into the background.

In the ocean, there's a second advantage. A predator looking down at a fish sees its dark back against the dark deep water. A predator looking up from below sees its pale belly against the bright surface.

Interestingly, some animals that spend their lives upside down, like a certain catfish that swims belly up, have the pattern reversed. Their bellies are darker than their backs, which actually supports the idea that the pattern is about the direction of light.

options: How sharks and other predators hunt fish

optionNotes: Predators are mentioned only to explain the pattern's advantage.

Dark deep water is a detail, not the topic.
Correct. The talk explains countershading and why it works as camouflage.
questions.explanation: The professor defines countershading, explains why it hides animals and gives evidence for the explanation.

options: Its colors are brighter than the background.

optionNotes: Bright colors are not discussed.
Correct. The shadow makes the body look solid and therefore visible.
That describes countershading itself, which makes animals harder to see.
Movement is not mentioned.
questions.explanation: Light from above leaves the belly in shadow, which makes the body look solid and stand out.
questions.evidence: That shadow makes the animal look solid and three-dimensional, which makes it easier to see.

options: Its dark back matches the dark water below it.

optionNotes: Correct. From above, the dark back blends with the dark deep water.

questions.explanation: A predator looking down sees the dark back against dark deep water.
questions.evidence: A predator looking down at a fish sees its dark back against the dark deep water.

options: To give an exception that weakens the explanation
To show that catfish have few predators
To support the idea that the pattern is related to the direction of light
To introduce a different kind of camouflage
optionNotes: It looks like an exception, but the professor says it actually supports the explanation.
Catfish predators are not discussed.
Correct. Its reversed pattern still puts the dark side toward the light.
It is still countershading, just reversed.
questions.explanation: The upside-down catfish has a darker belly, which faces the light, confirming the light-direction explanation.
questions.evidence: which actually supports the idea that the pattern is about the direction of light

title: Why Mars is red
context: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.

lines.t: Let's start with a simple question: why is Mars red? Students often guess that it's hot, but Mars is actually much colder than Earth.

The real answer is rust. The surface of Mars is covered in dust and rock that contain a lot of iron. Over a very long time, that iron reacted with small amounts of oxygen and became iron oxide, which is the same material as the rust on an old bicycle.
Now, the color isn't just on the ground. Winds on Mars lift this fine dust into the air, so even the sky often looks pinkish or butterscotch in photographs taken by robots on the surface.
Here's something that surprises people. If you dig just a few centimeters under the surface, the rock is often grey, not red. The rusty layer is quite thin, a bit like a coat of paint.

We know this partly because the rovers have drilled into rocks, and the powder that came out was grey. That tells scientists that the red color is mainly a surface effect, caused by long exposure to the Martian environment.
Next time, we'll look at where that oxygen might have come from, which is still being debated.

optionNotes: Correct. The whole talk explains why Mars looks red.
Drilling is mentioned only as evidence.
The temperature is mentioned only to reject a wrong guess.
That is the topic of the next class.
questions.explanation: The professor explains that rusted iron in surface dust and rock makes Mars red.

options: The high temperature of the surface

optionNotes: She says Mars is actually much colder than Earth.
Correct. The iron became iron oxide, or rust.
The sky looks pinkish because of the dust, not the other way around.
The dust comes from Mars itself.
questions.explanation: Iron in the surface reacted with oxygen and became iron oxide, the same material as rust.
questions.evidence: that iron reacted with small amounts of oxygen and became iron oxide

optionNotes: Seasons are not mentioned.

Correct. Just a few centimeters down, the rock is grey.
The sky's color is explained earlier by wind-blown dust.
questions.explanation: The comparison stresses that the red rust is only a thin surface layer over grey rock.
questions.evidence: The rusty layer is quite thin, a bit like a coat of paint.

questions.explanation: The professor ends by saying the next class will look at where the oxygen came from.
questions.evidence: we'll look at where that oxygen might have come from

title: The paint tube and Impressionism
context: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.

lines.t: When we talk about the Impressionists, we usually focus on their style: the quick brushstrokes, the bright colors, the interest in changing light. But today I want to talk about a piece of technology that made their work possible: the paint tube.

Before the eighteen-forties, artists, or their assistants, ground their own pigments and mixed them with oil in the studio. The paint was stored in pieces of animal bladder tied with string, and it dried out quickly once opened. So painting outdoors for hours was very impractical.

Then, in eighteen forty-one, an American portrait painter named John Rand invented a collapsible metal tube with a screw cap. Paint could now be carried easily, kept fresh, and squeezed out as needed.

This changed things a lot. Painters could set up an easel in a field or by a river and work directly in front of their subject. That's exactly what artists like Monet did. They wanted to capture how a scene looked at a particular moment, say, a haystack in the morning versus the same haystack at sunset.

Renoir is reported to have said that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. That may be an exaggeration, but it reminds us that artistic movements don't come only from ideas. Sometimes they depend on very practical inventions.

options: Artists stopped grinding their own pigments for health reasons.
Impressionist painters preferred to work in their studios.
John Rand was an important Impressionist painter.
A practical invention helped make an artistic style possible.
optionNotes: Health reasons are not mentioned.
The opposite: tubes let them paint outdoors.
Rand was a portrait painter who invented the tube; he is not called an Impressionist.
Correct. The paint tube allowed painters to work outdoors, which Impressionism depended on.
questions.explanation: The professor argues that the paint tube, a practical invention, made outdoor Impressionist painting possible.

options: Pigments were too expensive to buy.

optionNotes: Cost is not mentioned.
Correct. Paint stored in animal bladders dried out quickly once opened.
Metal tubes were the solution, not the problem.
No such rule is mentioned.
questions.explanation: Paint stored in animal bladders dried out quickly, which made long outdoor sessions impractical.
questions.evidence: it dried out quickly once opened

options: To describe the farm where Monet lived

optionNotes: Monet's home is not discussed.

Correct. The example shows them capturing a scene at a particular moment.

title: The strength of weak ties
context: Listen to part of a talk in a sociology class.

lines.t: Today's concept comes from a famous study in sociology about how people find jobs. It's called the strength of weak ties.

Let me define the terms first. Your strong ties are the people you're close to: family, best friends, people you see all the time. Weak ties are acquaintances: someone from your old school, a neighbor you chat with occasionally, a friend of a friend.

Now, you might expect that when people look for work, their close friends would be the most helpful. They care about you, after all. But in the original research, most people who found jobs through a personal contact had heard about the job from someone they saw only occasionally or rarely.

Why would that be? The explanation is about information. Your close friends tend to know the same people you know and hear the same news you hear. So they rarely tell you something new. Your acquaintances move in different circles, so they're more likely to know about opportunities you haven't heard of.
So does that mean close friends aren't useful at all in a job search?
Not at all. Close friends may be more willing to help once you know about a job, for example by recommending you. The point is that weak ties are especially valuable as a source of new information.

How companies choose which applicants to hire
optionNotes: Recommendations come up only in the answer to the student.
Correct. The talk explains why weak ties often lead people to jobs.
Losing contact is not discussed.
Hiring decisions are not discussed.
questions.explanation: The talk presents the 'strength of weak ties': acquaintances often provide new job information.

questions.explanation: Weak ties are acquaintances, such as an old schoolmate or a friend of a friend.
questions.evidence: Weak ties are acquaintances

questions.evidence: Your close friends tend to know the same people you know and hear the same news you hear.

title: How limestone caves form
context: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.

lines.t: Last week we talked about how water shapes the land's surface. Today, let's go underground and look at limestone caves.

Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, often from the shells of ancient sea creatures. On its own, pure water doesn't dissolve limestone very well. But rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from the air and, more importantly, from the soil, and this forms a weak acid called carbonic acid.

As this slightly acidic water seeps down through cracks in the limestone, it slowly dissolves the rock and widens the cracks. Over hundreds of thousands of years, the cracks can grow into tunnels and large chambers.

Now here's the interesting part. The same process that creates a cave also decorates it. When water carrying dissolved limestone drips from a cave ceiling, it comes into contact with the cave air and loses some carbon dioxide. When that happens, it can't hold as much dissolved mineral, so a tiny amount of calcium carbonate is left behind. Drop by drop, that builds a stalactite hanging from the ceiling.
Where the drops land on the floor, the same thing happens, building a stalagmite upward. Given enough time, the two may meet and form a column.
These formations grow incredibly slowly, often less than a millimeter per year, which is why touching them is discouraged: oils from your skin can stop their growth.

optionNotes: Damage from touching is a final detail only.
The origin of limestone is a brief detail.
Correct. The talk covers how caves form and how stalactites and stalagmites grow.
Seawater is not discussed.
questions.explanation: The professor explains how acidic water creates caves and how the same chemistry builds cave formations.

Correct. She says 'more importantly, from the soil'.

questions.evidence: from the air and, more importantly, from the soil

optionNotes: Correct. Losing carbon dioxide means the water cannot hold as much mineral.

title: Loss leaders
context: Listen to part of a talk in a business class.

lines.t: Today we're going to look at a pricing strategy you've almost certainly experienced as a shopper, even if you didn't know its name. It's called a loss leader.
A loss leader is a product that a store sells at a very low price, sometimes even below what the store paid for it. So the store loses money on every one it sells. Why would a business do that?

The idea is that the cheap product brings customers into the store. Once they're there, most people don't buy just one item. They pick up other things too, and the store makes a good profit on those other products.

A classic example is a supermarket selling milk or eggs very cheaply. People buy these items often, so they notice the low price, and they come in regularly. While they're shopping, they also buy bread, snacks, and cleaning products at normal prices.

But the strategy has risks. Some customers, sometimes called cherry pickers, visit several stores and buy only the discounted items. If too many shoppers behave like that, the store simply loses money.

That's why stores choose loss leaders carefully. They pick products that people need regularly, and they often put them at the back of the store, so customers have to walk past many other products to reach them.

title: Loanwords
context: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.

lines.t: Today we're looking at how languages borrow words from each other. Linguists call these borrowed words loanwords.
English is full of them. Ballet and restaurant come from French, kindergarten from German, and tsunami from Japanese. In fact, a large share of everyday English vocabulary was originally borrowed.

So why do languages borrow? There are two main reasons. The first is need. When speakers encounter a new object or idea, they often simply take the name along with the thing. Coffee and chocolate entered European languages this way, together with the products themselves.

The second reason is prestige. If speakers see another language as fashionable or powerful, they may borrow words even when they already have perfectly good ones. After the Norman Conquest of ten sixty-six, French was the language of the ruling class in England. That's why English has pairs like cow and beef. The animal in the field kept its old English name, but the meat served at the tables of French-speaking nobles got a French name.

One more thing: borrowed words usually change to fit their new language. Speakers adjust the pronunciation to sounds they already use, and they apply their own grammar. English speakers say tsunamis, with an s for the plural, even though Japanese doesn't mark plurals that way.

title: The urban heat island
context: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.

lines.t: Let's turn to a phenomenon that's become central to city planning: the urban heat island. Simply put, cities tend to be warmer than the surrounding countryside, sometimes by several degrees, and the difference is usually greatest at night, not during the day.

Several factors contribute. First, materials. Asphalt and concrete absorb a great deal of solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after sunset. Second, the loss of vegetation. Plants cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration, essentially releasing water vapor, which uses up heat energy. Replace a park with a parking lot, and you lose that cooling. Third, geometry. Tall buildings lining narrow streets trap heat, because energy reflected off one wall simply hits another rather than escaping to the sky.
And then there's waste heat from human activity: vehicles, industry, and, ironically, air conditioners, which pump heat out of buildings and into the street.

Now, mitigation. Cities have experimented with cool roofs, coated to reflect sunlight, and with planting street trees. Trees are interesting because their benefit goes beyond shade. A single mature tree can transpire hundreds of liters of water on a hot day. But trees need water, and in drought-prone cities that creates a genuine trade-off, so planners can't simply plant their way out of the problem.
